title: Logic: Arguments, Validity, and the Art of Reasoning

questions.question: In the philosophical sense, an argument is:
options: A heated exchange between two people
A set of premises offered in support of a conclusion
A statement that is always true
A claim that appeals to emotion
questions.rationale: Philosophers define an argument as premises offered as reasons for accepting a conclusion — not a quarrel.

questions.question: Which kind of inference reasons from an observed effect to its most plausible explanation?
questions.rationale: Abduction is inference to the best explanation, e.g. 'the lawn is wet; probably it rained'. Deduction applies rules with necessity; induction generalises from observed cases.

questions.question: A deductive argument that is valid but has a false premise is:
questions.rationale: Soundness requires both a valid form AND premises that are actually true. A valid argument with a false premise proves nothing.

questions.question: 'If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is dry. Therefore, it did not rain.' This is which form?
questions.rationale: Modus tollens has the pattern: If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. Here the consequent (wet ground) is denied, so the antecedent (rain) is denied.

questions.question: 'If the battery is dead, the car will not start. The car did not start. Therefore the battery is dead.' This reasoning is:
questions.rationale: The form is 'If P then Q; Q; so P' — affirming the consequent. Other causes (empty fuel, broken starter) could make the car not start, so the form is invalid.

questions.question: The rooster crows just before sunrise, so the crowing must cause the sunrise. This is which fallacy?
questions.rationale: Post hoc assumes that because one thing follows another, it was caused by it — mere succession is not causation.

questions.question: An argument can have true premises and a false conclusion only when:
questions.rationale: By definition, a valid deductive argument cannot have true premises and a false conclusion. So the 'some cats / some black things' example fails only because its form is invalid.

questions.question: 'You are with us or against us' commits which fallacy?
questions.rationale: A false dilemma hides live options, presenting only two alternatives when more exist.

questions.question: Begging the question is the fallacy of:
options: Assuming what the argument must prove
Attacking the speaker instead of the argument
questions.rationale: 'This book is true because the book says so' assumes the very conclusion in question. Attacking the speaker is ad hominem; popularity is bandwagon.

questions.question: On the square of opposition, the universal affirmative 'All S are P' (A) is the contradictory of:
options: The universal negative 'No S are P' (E)
The particular negative 'Some S are not P' (O)
The particular affirmative 'Some S are P' (I)
questions.rationale: A and O are contradictories — exactly one is true. A and E are contraries (both cannot be true), while A entails I.
